$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-\frac{1}{2}x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

$$
y=0
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line.

Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

$$
y=x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14149541/assets/c675f557abede7c8f21eadf3fd65dbd522c5ee9ad0a4ed0a804b03f357c1dc3b.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

$$
y=2x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14149541/assets/a25c57a021e42b2fa78b71f9ab79f0676a16f7c4f1082af0e9502d4d63ed4e46.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are negative. The eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue) is the one closest to $0.$

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{2}$ as they move towards the origin, the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior is ${\lambda }_{2}.$

Therefore, ${\lambda }_{1}<{\lambda }_{2}<0.$

questions.worked_solution:
The straight-line solutions of the system have the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

$$
y=\frac{1}{2}x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14149541/assets/abdb72ad4cd1bbde4e53c901b6b285904078f456a3fa52ab667bf1675d2d68dd.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation

$$
y=-x,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14149541/assets/cf3cb4b5756e5f382cd798d371e3d3e797f5ba0a146cdb8424ed1c62c051564b.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing $\text{toward the origin},$ meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are negative. The eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue) is the one closest to $0.$

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move towards the origin, the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior is ${\lambda }_{1}.$

Therefore, ${\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}<0.$
